case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress may constitutionally bar an individual who is an “unlawful user of” controlled substances from possessing a firearm under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), consistent with the Second Amendment’s text-and-history test.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II (as interpreted under New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen) and 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by a person who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because historical tradition supports disarming persons whose condition or conduct makes them dangerous or unreliable with weapons—particularly by analogy to longstanding regulations restricting armed intoxication and other status-based restrictions tied to public safety. The government emphasizes that the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively invalidates most real-world applications of § 922(g)(3), creates a deep circuit split, and undermines an important and frequently used federal firearm-prohibition aimed at preventing gun violence involving habitual illegal drug users even when not proven intoxicated at the precise moment of possession.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied because the government cannot satisfy Bruen’s historical-analogue requirement for a broad, status-based prohibition on mere possession by an “unlawful user” who is not shown to be intoxicated or otherwise dangerous at the time of firearm possession. Respondent (and supporting amici) contend that historical laws about intoxication were narrow, conduct-focused, and temporally limited (e.g., restricting carrying/using guns while actually intoxicated), and therefore are not sufficiently analogous to a modern categorical ban that turns on a fluid status like “unlawful user,” potentially sweeping in nonviolent people without individualized proof of dangerousness.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va.; aff’d 4th Cir.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas are right to insist that founding-era intoxication laws were conduct- and time-limited and that surety/going-armed regimes typically involved individualized process; that mismatch in “how” raises serious overbreadth concerns if § 922(g)(3) is read as an open-ended status ban untethered to contemporaneous impairment. But as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, in this posture a facial challenge fails under Salerno so long as the Government has shown at least some constitutional applications, and the statute’s present-tense terms support a limiting construction tied to ongoing, contemporaneous unlawful use during the period of possession. Under Bruen’s analogical method, those core applications are relevantly similar in why and how to the historical tradition of restricting arms use when a present condition of impairment elevates risk, without demanding a historical twin. The appropriate course is therefore to reverse the facial invalidation and leave room for as-applied challenges at the margins where temporality, proof of ongoing use, or nexus to impairment is lacking—addressing the respondents’ best point without converting Bruen into a one-to-one matching test.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press that § 922(g)(3) can be saved by construing it as a present-tense, temporally bounded disability, and Justice Gorsuch adds that any constitutional applications defeat facial relief under Salerno. But Bruen’s inquiry is not satisfied by redescribing a categorical, convictionless possession ban as an “impairment proxy” untethered to intoxication at the time of possession and lacking the individualized, process-protective features that characterized surety and going-armed regimes; the mismatch in “how” is decisive. The founding-era intoxication laws regulated the act of being armed while actually intoxicated, not the broader status of being an “unlawful user,” and importing an abstract dangerousness principle at that level of generality is exactly the interest-balancing-by-proxy Bruen forbids. On this record—litigated and resolved as applied—I would affirm as applied and leave Congress to craft a historically grounded, procedurally cabined alternative if it wishes to address contemporaneous impairment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas rightly underscore that founding-era analogues most clearly targeted the act of being armed while actually intoxicated, and that Bruen does not authorize a free-floating “dangerousness” inquiry divorced from the historically accepted mechanisms of regulation. But I agree with the Chief Justice that Bruen’s analogical test does not demand a historical twin, and that—construed according to its present-tense terms—§ 922(g)(3) can be applied in a temporally bounded way to contemporaneous, regular unlawful use during the period of possession, making it relevantly similar in “why” and “how” to the impairment tradition rather than a permanent status disarmament. Justice Gorsuch’s Salerno point further confirms that facial invalidation is unwarranted where at least some core applications fit within that historical tradition, even if marginal cases may present serious as-applied problems. The Fifth Circuit’s near one-to-one requirement is inconsistent with Bruen/Rahimi’s instruction to reason by relevant similarity rather than demanding an exact historical match.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s objection about the mismatch in “how”—Founding-era intoxication laws were contemporaneous and conduct-specific, and surety/going-armed regimes were process-bound—squarely targets the statute’s indeterminacy and the risk of converting history into an abstract “dangerousness” power. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Bruen (and Rahimi) asks for relevant similarity, not a historical twin, and our tradition permits preventive, condition-linked restraints when the government targets a credible threat to others’ physical safety. Properly construed in its present tense and applied to contemporaneous, regular unlawful use during the period of possession, § 922(g)(3) operates as a bounded, temporary disability keyed to ongoing impairment risk, not a broad, permanent divestment—enough to defeat the Fifth Circuit’s facial invalidation (as Justice Gorsuch’s Salerno point underscores) while preserving room for as-applied challenges at the statute’s margins.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas have the hardest point: the best founding analogues regulate the act of being armed while intoxicated (and surety regimes involved some process), so § 922(g)(3) cannot be upheld by invoking a free-floating “dangerousness” power. But the statute’s own text matters: Congress chose a present-tense trigger—someone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to”—which is most naturally read, as the Chief Justice argues, to require ongoing, contemporaneous unlawful use during the period of possession, making the restriction temporary and condition-linked rather than a permanent status disability. Under Bruen/Rahimi’s “why” and “how” inquiry, that narrow construction aligns the law with the historical tradition of restricting arms where a present condition (intoxication/impairment) heightens the risk of misuse, even if the Founding wrote the rule as a conduct prohibition rather than our modern proxy. And on Justice Gorsuch’s point about posture, those core applications are enough to defeat the Fifth Circuit’s facial invalidation, leaving the statute’s imprecise margins for as-applied challenges where temporality or nexus to impairment is not proved.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the hardest point: the best founding-era analogues targeted the act of being armed while actually intoxicated, and surety regimes typically required some individualized process—so § 922(g)(3) risks operating as an untethered status disability lacking the same “how.” But in this facial posture, Salerno matters: as the Chief Justice explains, the Government need only identify some constitutional applications, and § 922(g)(3) can be valid when construed and proved as contemporaneous, ongoing unlawful use during the period of possession, making the restraint temporary and condition-linked rather than permanent. Bruen’s analogical inquiry does not demand a historical twin; those core applications are relevantly similar in why and how to historical intoxication-based restrictions, even if marginal applications (where temporality, proof, or nexus to impairment is missing) remain open to as-applied challenges. For that reason I would reverse the facial invalidation while expressly reserving room for as-applied litigation at the statute’s edges.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas raise the strongest objection: Founding-era analogues most clearly targeted the act of being armed while actually intoxicated, and surety/going-armed regimes often required a complaint and individualized process—features that do not map neatly onto a categorical, status-based label like “unlawful user.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Bruen (and Rahimi) do not require a historical twin; the proper question is relevant similarity in “why” and “how,” and § 922(g)(3) is best construed in its present-tense terms as temporally bounded to ongoing, contemporaneous unlawful use—functioning as a proxy for recurrent impairment and heightened misuse risk rather than a permanent forfeiture. In this facial posture, Justice Gorsuch’s Salerno point is significant: because there are plainly constitutional applications where the Government proves contemporaneous, regular unlawful use during the period of possession, the Fifth Circuit’s facial invalidation goes too far. Concerns about imprecision and overbreadth are better handled through as-applied challenges requiring proof of ongoing use sufficiently tied to the time of possession, rather than a decision that effectively overrides Congress’s categorical risk judgment across the board.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan make the Government’s strongest point: the present-tense phrasing—someone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to”—can be read to target ongoing, contemporaneous use and thus look more like historical restrictions on carrying while actually intoxicated. But Bruen’s analogical inquiry turns on “how” as well as “why,” and the founding-era analogues they invoke were conduct- and moment-specific (armed while intoxicated) or procedurally cabined (surety/going-armed after a complaint and individualized showing), whereas § 922(g)(3) imposes a categorical possession ban triggered by an indeterminate status label untethered to impairment at the time of possession. Justice Gorsuch’s Salerno posture argument is substantial, yet this case has been litigated and decided as applied, and I am not persuaded we should recharacterize it to avoid asking whether this mechanism of disarmament has an adequate historical analogue on this record. I would therefore affirm as applied here while leaving open narrower applications where contemporaneous impairment during possession is proved and the statute operates as a truly time-bound proxy for the historical intoxication restriction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s point that § 922(g)(3) can be read as present-tense and thus “temporally bounded,” and Justice Gorsuch’s Salerno posture argument would have force if the case truly turned on a facial attack. But even under that narrowing construction, the Government’s historical analogues regulate the contemporaneous risky act (armed while intoxicated) or impose conditional restraints after an individualized, process-protective showing—features missing from an open-ended possession ban keyed to the indeterminate status of being an “unlawful user.” As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, allowing “danger-linked” principles at that level of abstraction lets legislatures convert time-limited conduct rules into broad status disarmaments without the procedural safeguards that historically constrained preventive measures. Given the practical consequences of § 922(g)(3)’s imprecision and enforcement discretion on this record, I remain unpersuaded the Government has carried its Bruen/Rahimi burden as applied here.

John Roberts.reasoning: This case, properly understood, is at least an as-applied challenge, and under Bruen the question is whether disarming this defendant as an “unlawful user” is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. History supports temporarily restricting firearm access for those whose ongoing condition makes them dangerous or unreliable with weapons—by analogy to regulations addressing armed intoxication and to surety/going-armed regimes that imposed weapon-related burdens based on a demonstrated risk to public safety. Section 922(g)(3), as applied here to a regular, contemporaneous unlawful user, is sufficiently bounded to operate as a danger-linked, conditional disarmament rather than a permanent, categorical deprivation untethered to risk. Whatever harder questions may arise at the statute’s margins given the term’s temporal imprecision, the Government has shown at least some constitutional applications, and this application fits within the historical principle of disarming persons whose impairment makes firearm possession especially hazardous.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers the conduct at issue—mere possession of a firearm by an ordinary member of “the people”—so § 922(g)(3) is presumptively unconstitutional as applied absent a historically grounded analogue. The Government’s proffered history (laws punishing or restricting the carrying or use of arms while actually intoxicated) is conduct- and time-limited, and thus does not justify a categorical, status-based disarmament keyed to the fluid label “unlawful user” (often extending well beyond any moment of intoxication and without a conviction-based trigger). Bruen forbids substituting an abstract “dangerousness” rationale for the required showing that the specific mechanism of disarmament has a founding-era tradition; here, the statute’s breadth and indeterminate trigger dilute the right to keep arms for self-defense in a way the Government has not shown to be consistent with that tradition. Because the Government cannot carry its historical burden, § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional on these facts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen, the question is whether § 922(g)(3), as applied to a person who is an ongoing “unlawful user” of controlled substances, fits within the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, not whether it advances public-safety interests under means-end scrutiny. The historical record contains enduring analogues for temporarily disarming those whose condition makes them dangerous or incapable of responsible arms use—most notably regulations restricting armed intoxication and other measures aimed at persons whose impaired judgment posed an acute risk—supporting Congress’s judgment that habitual unlawful drug use is sufficiently analogous to such impairment-based restrictions. While the historical laws often targeted conduct contemporaneous with intoxication, Bruen allows analogical reasoning at the level of “how” and “why,” and here the “why” (preventing armed use by persons with materially impaired judgment) and “how” (disarming a definable class during the period of impairment/ongoing use) align closely enough to sustain the statute’s application. Rejecting that tradition in favor of individualized, case-by-case dangerousness determinations would invite the kind of open-ended judicial discretion Bruen sought to foreclose and would functionally nullify a categorical prohibition Congress enacted without such an exception.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Bruen, the question is whether § 922(g)(3)’s temporary bar on firearm possession by an “unlawful user” is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, assessed through relevant analogues rather than a precise match. Historical surety and “going armed” traditions reflect a longstanding practice of restricting arms for those whose condition or conduct poses a credible threat to others’ physical safety, and founding-era regulations targeting intoxication and habitual drunkenness show that lawmakers treated impaired or chronically impaired persons as uniquely dangerous and subject to preventive restraints more severe than a time-limited disarmament. As applied here, the statute does not “broadly divest” the right in perpetuity; it operates as a targeted, criteria-bound restriction tied to ongoing unlawful drug use that reasonably tracks the historic justification of preventing armed violence by persons whose judgment and self-control are compromised. The Fifth Circuit’s demand for a near one-to-one historical match misconceives Bruen’s analogical inquiry and would disable a traditional category of preventive firearm regulation aimed at credible threats to public safety.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the text and its target: § 922(g)(3) bars firearm possession by a person who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances—language Congress chose to address a continuing condition, not a one-off episode, and the obvious fit is to prevent guns in the hands of those whose repeated illegal drug use makes safe handling and judgment unreliable. Under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi, the Government need not produce a historical “twin”; it must show a relevantly similar tradition of disarming or restricting arms for persons posing a special danger of misuse, and the Nation’s longstanding practice of regulating armed intoxication and comparable public-safety disabilities supports that general principle even if the historical laws were often time-limited in form. Applying ordinary merits discipline to the facts here, the record reflects habitual unlawful drug use during the period of possession—so the statute’s status element is satisfied in a way that tracks Congress’s danger-focused rationale rather than sweeping in a remote or purely technical user. Because the Fifth Circuit’s demand for a near-exact historical analogue for this particular modern category reads Bruen at too fine a level of generality, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied and reverse.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text presumptively covers keeping and possessing ordinary firearms, so the government bears the burden under Bruen to show § 922(g)(3)’s disarmament of an “unlawful user” accords with this Nation’s historical tradition. In this posture, however, respondent’s facial challenge runs headlong into Salerno: he must show “no set of circumstances” exists in which § 922(g)(3) can be constitutionally applied, and the government can at least identify historically grounded analogues for temporarily disarming persons whose current condition renders them dangerous or unreliable with arms—such as restrictions tied to intoxication and other forms of mental impairment posing an acute risk. That suffices to defeat a facial attack even if the statute’s breadth (its fluid “unlawful user” status, duration, and lack of individualized findings) may invite serious as-applied challenges in particular circumstances where dangerousness and temporariness are not shown. Because some constitutional applications remain, I would reverse the invalidation here and leave the harder line-drawing to as-applied litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying the Heller/Bruen framework of text, history, and precedent, the Second Amendment protects “the people” but has always been subject to “important limitations,” including historically recognized restrictions tied to public safety and disarming categories of persons deemed dangerous or unreliable. As applied to an individual who is an “unlawful user of” controlled substances in an ongoing, habitual sense, § 922(g)(3) fits within the historical tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose condition or conduct makes firearm misuse more likely, even if Founding-era regulations often operated through prohibitions on armed intoxication and other danger-linked restrictions rather than modern status labels. Congress’s categorical judgment that habitual illegal drug use correlates with impaired judgment and heightened risk is a policy determination courts should not lightly override where the statute’s application is cabined to current unlawful users (not a lifetime ban), and the defendant remains free to raise an as-applied challenge if the government cannot prove contemporaneous, regular use sufficient to establish “unlawful user” status. In that posture, the statute operates as a historically grounded, risk-based disarmament measure rather than an open-ended deprivation untethered from dangerousness.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, the threshold question is whether § 922(g)(3) as applied regulates conduct covered by the Second Amendment’s text; possession of a firearm by an ordinary citizen falls within “keep and bear Arms,” so the burden shifts to the Government to show a sufficiently analogous historical tradition. The Government’s primary analogues—laws punishing or restricting armed intoxication—are temporally and conduct limited (aimed at being armed while actually intoxicated), and they do not establish a founding-era tradition of disarming a person based on the more indeterminate status of being an “unlawful user” absent proof of contemporaneous impairment or a demonstrated propensity for violence. Rahimi allows legislatures to disarm categories who pose a “special danger of misuse,” but it does not dispense with Bruen’s demand for a genuinely comparable historical justification-and-scope fit; on this record, the Government has not shown a tradition supporting a categorical, ongoing possession ban keyed to drug use untethered to intoxication at the time of gun possession. Because the Government’s argument relies too heavily on general “dangerousness” at a level of abstraction that risks substituting expected applications for original meaning, I would affirm as applied here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework with an eye toward procedural fairness and real-world consequences, § 922(g)(3) as applied here sweeps too broadly because it hinges on a fluid status (“unlawful user”) without requiring proof that the individual was actually intoxicated, impaired, or otherwise dangerous at the time of possession. The historical materials the Government invokes—rules against carrying or firing while intoxicated and other public-safety measures—are materially narrower and conduct-focused, and thus do not supply a sufficiently analogous tradition for a categorical, ongoing possession ban untethered to contemporaneous impairment or individualized dangerousness. That mismatch, combined with the statute’s vagueness-like practical operation (risking uneven enforcement against nonviolent defendants), counsels against upholding this application under the Second Amendment. Congress may regulate firearms to protect public safety, but under Bruen the Government must show a closer historical fit than generalized “dangerousness” analogies when the law disarms people based on status rather than proven risky conduct.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress may constitutionally prohibit firearm possession by a person who is an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) consistent with the Second Amendment’s text-and-history test.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. II; 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (ban on firearm possession by anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied to Hemani because the Second Amendment permits disarming persons whose habitual drug use makes them comparably risky or non-law-abiding under historical analogues; history shows a longstanding tradition of temporarily disarming dangerous or impaired persons (e.g., intoxication-based restrictions and other public-safety regulations), and modern drug-use disarmament is relevantly similar in burden and justification. The government also stresses that the Fifth Circuit effectively invalidated most applications of an often-used federal statute, deepening a circuit conflict (including with later decisions like the Third Circuit’s Harris), and that Bruen does not require a historical twin—only a sufficiently analogous tradition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied because the government cannot identify a well-established Founding-era tradition of categorically disarming people based solely on unlawful drug use (especially when not intoxicated at the time of possession). Under Bruen, respondent contends, analogies to narrow intoxication-in-public or misuse laws are insufficient to justify a broad status-based ban that operates even when the person is sober, peaceable, and not shown to be dangerous; thus the statute, at least in most applications like his, lacks the required historical grounding and impermissibly burdens protected conduct.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Assn., Inc. v. Bruen (2022)
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va. 2023), aff’d (4th Cir. 2025), cert. denied (2025)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to stress that many historical intoxication laws were conduct-based and keyed to contemporaneous impairment, and that Bruen forbids open-ended risk balancing untethered to history. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh explain, Bruen and Rahimi ask for a relevantly similar analogue in why and how the burden operates, not a founding-era “twin,” and § 922(g)(3) is written in the present tense and functions as a temporary disability tied to ongoing unlawful use or addiction—i.e., a condition Congress could reasonably treat as elevating misuse risk. Justice Sotomayor’s point about surety and going-armed laws having individualized procedures highlights possible overbreadth in marginal cases, but in this posture we can resolve only Hemani’s application (or, if treated as facial, apply Salerno) and avoid endorsing any free-floating “non-law-abiding” carveout. A narrow opinion sustaining the statute as applied to a current, habitual unlawful user best fits the historical tradition of temporarily disarming those whose ongoing condition makes armed misuse more likely while leaving harder applications for another day.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers Hemani’s possession, so the Government must identify a Founding-era tradition supporting this kind of categorical, status-based disarmament. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s appeal to a general principle of temporarily disarming those deemed risky because of an “ongoing condition” is pitched at too high a level of generality and effectively reintroduces interest-balancing that Bruen rejected by letting legislatures define the right’s boundaries through contemporary risk assessments. The historical materials they invoke—intoxication laws and related public-safety measures—are chiefly conduct-based (carrying/using while actually intoxicated) or individualized (surety/going-armed), as Justice Sotomayor notes, and thus do not justify an automatic ban that applies even when one is sober and without any judicial finding. Nor does calling the disability “temporary” solve the problem: absent a well-established historical analogue for disarming nonconvicted persons based on a status label untethered to adjudicated misconduct, § 922(g)(3) as applied remains inconsistent with the Nation’s tradition.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that many Founding-era laws targeted carrying or firing while actually intoxicated, not a possession ban that persists when the person is sober. But that reads Bruen/Rahimi too rigidly: as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the inquiry is relevant similarity in why and how the burden operates, and § 922(g)(3) is expressly tied to a present-tense, ongoing condition—current unlawful use or addiction—so it functions as a temporary disarmament keyed to heightened misuse risk rather than a permanent status disability. Justice Sotomayor’s demand for an individualized, judicial dangerousness finding imports a procedural requirement the historical record does not uniformly impose and would make Congress’s preventive judgments administratively unworkable in a context where delay can be fatal. On these facts, the Government has shown a sufficiently close analogue in the tradition of time-limited disarmament of those whose ongoing condition or course of unlawful conduct makes armed possession unusually dangerous.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Bruen does not demand a historical “twin,” and that § 922(g)(3) is framed in the present tense and can operate temporally. But their best analogy—temporary disarmament of the intoxicated or otherwise dangerous—still fails on the historical “how”: the principal Founding-era mechanisms we have (surety laws and “going armed” offenses) turned on an individualized, judicially grounded showing of a credible threat, and intoxication restrictions targeted armed conduct while actually impaired, not categorical possession by a person who may be sober and has no danger finding. Justice Alito’s concern about administrability cannot supply the missing historical fit; Bruen’s test asks whether the burden and its justification are consistent with tradition, and here the tradition reflects calibrated, threat-based interventions rather than an automatic, status-triggered disability. On this record, I would hold § 922(g)(3) unconstitutional as applied to Hemani absent evidence tying his firearm possession to demonstrated dangerousness akin to what history required.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor make the case’s hardest point: the closest Founding-era analogues often regulated carrying while actually intoxicated or required an individualized surety/going-armed proceeding, not a categorical possession ban that can apply when a person is sober. But § 922(g)(3)’s operative, present-tense text—“is an unlawful user of or addicted to”—already supplies the limiting principle the Fifth Circuit largely ignored, making the prohibition function as a temporary, condition-linked disarmament rather than a permanent status mark. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Bruen (especially after Rahimi) does not demand a historical twin; it asks whether the modern law is relevantly similar in burden and justification, and disarming those with an ongoing impairment-linked condition that elevates misuse risk fits within that tradition at the right level of generality. And in this as-applied posture, we can uphold the statute on these facts without endorsing its outermost applications or requiring Congress to replicate surety’s procedural form.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor are right to insist that many historical analogues were episodic (intoxication-in-the-moment) or individualized (surety/going-armed) rather than categorical status disabilities, and that we must avoid converting “dangerousness” into a free-floating legislative license. But this remains a facial challenge, and under Salerno the question is whether § 922(g)(3) has at least some constitutional applications; as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the statute is temporally keyed to present unlawful use or addiction, not a permanent disarmament based on a remote episode. On that narrower understanding, the government’s history—temporary disarmament tied to an ongoing condition that heightens misuse risk—suffices to defeat facial invalidation, while leaving open the harder as-applied cases Justice Sotomayor flags (sporadic or past use, lack of evidence of ongoing impairment, self-defense circumstances). I would thus vote to reverse while making clear we are not endorsing categorical disarmament untethered to historically comparable limiting features.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest objection: Founding-era intoxication restrictions were typically conduct-based (carrying/using while actually intoxicated) and surety regimes were individualized and judicially mediated. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Bruen (and Rahimi) asks for a relevantly similar analogue in burden and justification, not a historical twin, and § 922(g)(3) as applied here functions as a temporary, present-tense disarmament tied to ongoing unlawful use/addiction rather than a permanent ban based on remote conduct. The statute’s justification—reducing the risk of armed misuse by persons whose ongoing condition makes them unreliable—fits within the historical tradition of disarming those understood to pose a special danger, even if earlier laws often operationalized that judgment through different mechanisms. I would not endorse a free-floating “not law-abiding” test, but on these facts the Fifth Circuit demanded too much historical identity and too little analogical reasoning.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist that Bruen cannot be satisfied by an abstract “dangerousness” label that lets modern risk assessments supplant history, and Justice Sotomayor is right that surety/going-armed laws often involved individualized, judicially mediated constraints. But § 922(g)(3)’s enacted text matters: it is keyed to a present-tense condition—one who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to”—so the Fifth Circuit’s framing of the statute as a categorical ban on sober people overreads it and dilutes the temporal limitation Congress chose. Consistent with the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s point, Bruen (as clarified in Rahimi) asks for a relevantly similar tradition in why and how, and the historical record of temporary disarmament tied to impairment-linked conditions supports at least this as-applied application to an ongoing unlawful user without deciding marginal cases. On this record, I do not think the respondent has shown the mismatch is so stark that we must invalidate the statute as applied here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Sotomayor rightly press that many Founding-era laws regulated firearm use while actually intoxicated, and that surety/going-armed regimes were often individualized and judicially mediated. But § 922(g)(3)’s text is not a permanent, status-based disarmament untethered to conduct; it applies only to one who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to” a controlled substance as Congress defined that term by cross-reference to the federal schedules, a deliberately temporal design that keys the disability to a present condition and lifts when that condition ends. Under Bruen’s analogical inquiry (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize), the government need not supply a historical twin, and the tradition of temporarily separating arms from persons whose ongoing condition makes misuse unusually likely supplies the relevantly similar “why” and “how” in this as-applied posture. Justice Sotomayor’s preference for an individualized danger finding may be sensible as policy, but absent a textual or historical requirement that Congress must proceed only through case-by-case adjudication, I do not think our role permits rewriting the line Congress drew to mirror surety procedures.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen, the Government must justify § 922(g)(3) by showing it fits within the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation, and that inquiry turns on whether the restriction targets persons understood to pose a special danger of misuse. As applied to Hemani—an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances as Congress defined that term—the prohibition is temporary and status-linked to ongoing impairment and lawbreaking, and it is relevantly analogous in justification to historical measures that disarmed dangerous or impaired persons and those whose condition made armed misuse more likely. Heller’s recognition that certain disarmament laws are “presumptively lawful” reinforces that legislatures have authority to bar possession by categories of persons thought to present heightened risk, and Bruen does not demand a historical twin so long as the modern law is comparably justified and burdensome. Procedurally, because Hemani brings an as-applied challenge, the Government need only show the statute’s constitutionality in this application, not defend every conceivable edge case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text covers Hemani’s conduct—possessing a firearm—so the conduct is presumptively protected and the Government bears the burden to justify § 922(g)(3) by reference to this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. The Government’s asserted analogues (e.g., narrow laws addressing carrying or firing while actually intoxicated, or other situational public-safety measures) regulate temporary impairment in particular places or moments; they do not establish a Founding-era tradition of a categorical, status-based disarmament triggered by “unlawful user” status even when the person is sober and not convicted of any disqualifying crime. Accepting the Government’s “dangerous/non-law-abiding” principle as sufficient would invite modern policy balancing to define away the right, contrary to the Second Amendment’s historically fixed scope and its unqualified command. Because the Government has not shown a sufficiently analogous historical tradition supporting this automatic disability as applied to Hemani, § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework as refined by Rahimi, § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the Nation’s tradition of temporarily disarming individuals whose condition makes firearm possession unusually dangerous, including those impaired or otherwise posing a heightened risk to public safety. The statute targets ongoing unlawful drug use or addiction—conduct that places the person outside the community of law-abiding, responsible citizens and is closely analogous in justification to historical regulations addressing intoxication and other dangerousness-based limitations. A categorical prohibition tied to current unlawful use is a practical, administrable means of preventing armed violence and accidents, and the Constitution does not require Congress to wait until the individual is literally intoxicated at the moment of possession. The Fifth Circuit’s contrary approach applies Bruen at an unduly narrow level of generality and would destabilize longstanding public-safety regulations with predictable, harmful consequences.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework, the Government must show that disarming Hemani as an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances is consistent with historical regulatory principles, not merely that drug use is unlawful today. The surety and “going armed” traditions I have relied on support disarmament only after an individualized, judicially grounded showing that a person poses a “credible threat to the physical safety of others,” and they typically operated as temporary, calibrated restraints—not a broad, status-based prohibition untethered to contemporaneous impairment or a danger finding. Intoxication-era analogues, to the extent they exist, are closer to conduct-based limits on carrying or using arms while actively intoxicated, and they do not justify categorically barring firearm possession by someone who is sober and not shown on this record to be dangerous. On these facts, § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani lacks the historically grounded nexus to a demonstrated threat that our precedents treat as the touchstone for permissible disarmament.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with what § 922(g)(3) actually does: it targets a temporally limited status—being a current “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances—rather than permanently stripping arms from a broad class, and Congress drew that line to address the heightened risk of impaired judgment and gun misuse associated with ongoing drug use. Under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi, the question is not whether Founding-era legislatures used the identical category “unlawful drug user,” but whether the modern law is consistent with the principles underpinning historical firearm regulation—especially temporary disarmament of persons whose condition makes them dangerous or not reliably law-abiding, including intoxication-based restrictions and other public-safety measures. On these facts, where Hemani’s habitual unlawful drug use places him within the statute’s operative terms, the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively rewrites Bruen into a demand for a historical “twin” and would disable Congress from making the kind of calibrated, risk-based judgment it enacted here. Because the statute’s burden and justification are relevantly similar to historical traditions of disarming those posing an acute risk, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text covers Hemani’s possession of a firearm, so Bruen requires the government to show § 922(g)(3) aligns with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. In this posture, Hemani presses a facial challenge, and under Salerno that is “the most difficult challenge to mount successfully”: the government need only identify at least some constitutional applications, not justify every imaginable one. History reflects a tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose ongoing intoxication or comparable impairment poses a concrete risk—often with limiting features like transience and a focus on preventing misuse—features § 922(g)(3) plausibly shares at least as applied to a habitual unlawful drug user. Upholding the statute here would not resolve harder as-applied cases (e.g., sporadic use, remote use, or situations lacking evidence of contemporaneous impairment or dangerousness), but it suffices to defeat a facial invalidation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework, Hemani’s possession of a firearm is covered by the Second Amendment’s text, so the government must justify § 922(g)(3) by reference to the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. History reflects a longstanding tradition of temporarily disarming individuals whose ongoing intoxication or impairment makes them dangerous with weapons, and § 922(g)(3)—as applied to a habitual unlawful user or addict—operates as a similarly temporary, status-linked disarmament tied to current impairment risk rather than a permanent ban. Consistent with Heller and McDonald’s recognition that the right is not absolute and is subject to historically grounded exceptions, this targeted prohibition fits within the tradition of disarming dangerous or non-law-abiding persons, especially given that the disability lifts when the unlawful drug use stops. The Fifth Circuit’s contrary approach effectively demands a historical “twin” and reads Bruen too narrowly, whereas Bruen permits sufficiently analogous historical regulations in both burden and justification.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The threshold question under Bruen is whether Hemani’s conduct—possessing a firearm while being an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances—falls within the Second Amendment’s protection as originally understood, and history supports treating habitual intoxication or ongoing unlawful drug use as a condition that places a person outside the class of responsible, law-abiding citizens entitled to carry arms without restriction. The government need not produce a historical “twin”; it suffices to identify a relevantly similar tradition, and founding-era and Reconstruction-era regulations aimed at preventing armed public danger from impairment (and at disarming those posing a demonstrable risk) are comparably justified and impose a comparably temporary, status-linked burden when applied to a current, regular unlawful user rather than a merely past user. Hemani’s as-applied challenge fails on this record because the statute targets ongoing unlawful use that correlates with impaired judgment and heightened risk, aligning with the historical principle of disarming those whose condition makes armed carry dangerous, rather than resting on mere “expectations” untethered to constitutional meaning. Given Bruen’s instruction to reason by analogy using burden and justification, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with the text, § 922(g)(3) applies only to a person who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to” a “controlled substance,” a term Congress explicitly defined by cross-reference to the federal schedules; that choice reflects a legislative judgment that firearm possession by current unlawful users/addicts poses a public-safety risk, and courts are not free to replace that calibrated line with their own policy preferences about which drugs or users are “dangerous.” Under Bruen’s framework, the relevant historical inquiry is at an appropriate level of generality—whether there is a tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose condition or ongoing conduct renders them comparably risky or not law-abiding—and Founding- and Reconstruction-era regulations restricting arms access for the intoxicated or otherwise impaired support the constitutionality of a targeted, status-linked prohibition tied to current unlawful use. On these facts, where the prosecution rests on Hemani’s ongoing unlawful marijuana use (not a one-off past event), the statute operates as a temporally limited disarmament measure keyed to present impairment/risk, which is sufficiently analogous in burden and justification to those historical restrictions. Any narrower tailoring arguments about how best to measure dangerousness are for Congress, and the enacted text can be applied consistent with the Second Amendment as construed in Bruen.
